How Frances National Front is winning working-class voters. Support in bastions such as Hayange could decide fate of Le Pen presidential bid

In case of paywall.

Hayange, a former manufacturing town that is now a bastion of France’s National Front, is crammed with memories of former glories.

A 1,200-seat concert hall is getting derelict. An ornate church modelled after a Parisian landmark still looms over the town. Both were built with the help of the Wendel steelmaking family, long the town’s biggest employer, who occupied a nearby castle and also helped furnish Hayange with a clutch of schools and swimming pools.

But the Wendels left in 1978 and the last of the steel furnaces closed three years ago.

The town’s story could serve as a template for the FN’s national efforts ahead of next year’s presidential elections, when Marine Le Pen, the party’s leader, is expected to qualify for the second round run-off.

“The future isn’t so promising for young people any more,” says Delphine Nigro, a 77-year-old resident who wistfully remembers a golden era when there was plenty of work, even if the smoke from the furnaces left black dust on vegetable patches.

After deindustrialisation came the FN’s victory in 2014, when Hayange became one of 11 towns captured by the far-right party, prefiguring the populist wave that has shaken the continent, notably with Britain’s June vote to leave the EU.

Today Hayange, which in its heyday lured in immigrants from Italy and elsewhere, has become staunchly Eurosceptic.

The FN has built much of its success over the past two years on an effort to gain the support of working class voters. Whether Ms Le Pen can defy the pollsters who predict she will ultimately lose the presidential contest, or at least do better than expected, will largely depend on whether she can mobilise disenchanted blue-collar voters, whose turnout has tended to be low.

“The FN has become the party of the working class,” says Bruno Cautrès, a political sciences researcher at Paris-based Sciences Po Cevipof. “The party offers a double explanation for their malaise: Europe has failed to protect their jobs from globalisation and failed to protect their way of life from Muslim immigrants.”

Socialist president François Hollande confronted the extent of working class anger this week when steel trade unions snubbed his visit to the nearby town of Florange.

Fabien Engelmann, Hayange’s 37-year-old FN mayor, a former unionist and member of the Trotskyist Lutte Ouvrière party, exults that the party is rallying “nationalists” against the “internationalists and Europeanists”.

Nationwide, about 45 per cent of blue-collar workers and 38 per cent of unemployed people or youngsters looking for their first job say they are planning to vote for Ms Le Pen, according to the latest survey by Cevipof.

Those most likely to back the party share many characteristics with some Britons who voted to leave the EU: typically they are paid less, have lower levels of education and live in small to medium-sized towns near bigger cities.

There are some important differences: while British voters over 60 typically backed Brexit, older French voters are the least receptive to the FN’s plans to break with Brussels.

In Hayange, Euroscepticism has been made more acute by the relative success of nearby Luxembourg, which tempts away educated people, including Ms Nigro’s banker son. Across the border, jobs are plentiful and salaries higher, while petrol and cigarettes are cheaper.

“Europe was good when we were six members,” says Ugo Vaona, a 72-year-old former leftwing unionist turned FN sympathiser. “I’m disappointed at the left. Ultimately, Hollande is not deciding anything, it’s the world of finance and Brussels that rule.”

Philippe David, the former Socialist mayor defeated by Mr Engelmann after serving three mandates, says that dislodging the FN will be tough.

Voting for the far-right is no longer taboo and, seeking to establish credibility, Mr Engelmann has steered away from bold actions. His flagship measures are a free shuttle bus for the elderly. Some of his more symbolic initiatives have caused controversy, such as an annual pig fair, which critics says is fuelling Islamophobia or his attempts to evict a charity that helps migrants from municipal premises.

Europe’s migrant crisis has also added to unease in this corner of the Moselle. A few years ago, the government relocated migrants from the Balkans in a rundown hotel close to the church. The hotel was recently closed, but other migrants, from Africa and the Middle East, have been offered housing in another part of town.

Nelly Zdun, the town’s newsagent, says: “A lot of my clients tell me, ‘What’s the use of my French identity card? Those guys have a place to sleep, they are given food and money and I’m barely getting by’.”

Ms Zdun was born to an Italian mother. Her husband, a former professional footballer who now owns a café, is the son of Polish immigrants. Even so, she says she will vote for Ms Le Pen against Mr Hollande in next year’s presidential run-off. Starting work at 5.30am and finishing at 7.15pm, taking only a week off in the summer, she blames the Socialist president for increasing taxes and charges.

But she adds that she would vote for Nicolas Sarkozy, the former centre-right leader, against Ms Le Pen, or give a chance to Emmanuel Macron, Mr Hollande’s former economy minister.

Her comments are symptomatic of the volatile support for the FN in Hayange among voters disillusioned by the traditional left but tempted by other politicians offering a break with the status quo.

Yves Pierrot, a former headteacher, describes himself as a leftwing sympathiser and no fan of the FN. But he faults the Socialist government for its relatievely pro-business shift and what he sees as a lack of action against Islamist extremists.

Partly as a result, he sees Ms Le Pen as “the only one giving hope” and suggests that her election as president would prompt a salutary reaction from an inept political class.

“We really need to start out on new foundations,” Mr Pierrot says. “I don’t want to choose between cholera and the plague next year.”
